Before you build: how to make your agent stop repeating the same mistakes, and the mark that AI text now carries.

# [Teach Your Agent]{.flow} {.title}

## The friction you know

- One week in, you have corrected your agent on the same things again and again: naming style, the library you prefer, "keep functions short", "round money to two decimals"
- Every session starts from zero: the agent remembers [nothing]{.highlight} between sessions (Session X, the loop)
- Explaining the same thing five times is work you should not be doing

## Package the rules once

- Put your project rules in **one markdown file** in the repo: `AGENTS.md`
- What goes in: what the project is, the tools it uses, naming and style conventions, "any AI use lands in the README disclosure"
- Mistral Vibe reads it at every session start, automatically: write the rules once, stop repeating them

## Skills: instructions on demand

- A **skill** is the next step up: a folder with a `SKILL.md`, holding a name, a description, and instructions
- Rules apply [always]{.highlight}. A skill loads only when the task matches its description, so context stays lean until the moment it is needed
- Example: a `verify` skill for your project: read the diff, run it, test it on a case where you know the answer, report what you checked
- In your stack: `.vibe/skills/verify/SKILL.md` in the repo. Vibe loads it in the terminal and inside Zed's agent panel, same engine
- Vibe follows an open format, so skills you write here also work in other agents that adopt it

## Anatomy, briefly

```markdown
---
name: verify
description: Check changed code the way this project requires. Use after any code change.
---

- Read the diff line by line before running anything
- Run the code on a case where you know the correct answer
- Report what you checked and what the result was
```

. . .

Plain markdown you own, at `.vibe/skills/verify/SKILL.md`, versioned with the project like any other file.

## Write your own

- Any workflow you have explained to the agent [twice]{.highlight} deserves a skill
- Keep it short: a page of instructions, not an essay
- Prune it when the workflow changes: a stale skill misleads
- Downloading one? Vet it by [reading it]{.highlight}, not by how popular it is

## What not to hand over

- The parts you must be able to **defend at the demo**: design choices, the statistics, why this approach
- A file can carry conventions. It cannot carry your judgment, and the demo questions come to you, not to it

# [The Mark]{.flow} {.title}

## Could anyone tell?

- Your README carries an AI-disclosure section. Suppose you skipped it: could anyone [prove]{.highlight} that an AI wrote part of your work?
- Since August 2026, EU rules require providers to mark AI content machine-readably, and the major ones do
- The trick behind it is simple enough for three slides

## How a watermark hides in plain text

- Before each word, the model splits its vocabulary into a **green** and a **red** half, reshuffled at every step
- It then softly prefers green words. The text still reads completely normally
- By chance, a human writes about half green words. A model writes far more

## You already know the mechanism

- Session VI: the model picks a [likely]{.highlight} next token, never *the* next token
- A watermark is that choice, steered on purpose: green wins a little more often than chance
- Same next-token choice, one hidden thumb on the scale

## Who can actually detect it

- Detection is [counting]{.highlight}: one paragraph of marked text can push chance below 1 in 10 trillion
- But you need the secret key that decided which half was green
- In practice, only the provider can run the test

## What a mark proves (and does not)

- Proves: a model [processed]{.highlight} this text
- Does not prove: who did the work, or whether a human verified it
- Heavy editing can wash a mark out, and short snippets may not carry one, so an absence proves nothing

. . .

Presence without disclosure, though, looks exactly like what it is.

## Disclosure is part of the work

- The rules converged everywhere: AI cannot be an author, and its use gets disclosed
- Your README section says which tool, for what, and what you verified yourself
- That is [standard practice]{.highlight}, not a confession

# [Definition of Done]{.flow} {.title}

## Before you call it finished

- The repo runs from a fresh clone (cloned once more into an empty folder): `uv sync`, then your script
- The README says what it does, how to run it, and carries the **AI disclosure section**
- The commit history tells the story: small steps, messages that mean something
- `git status` is clean: all committed, nothing important ignored
- I am invited, and the link is on Moodle before your demo

. . .

:::{.callout-tip}
Run the fresh-clone test **today**, not on demo morning. It always finds something.
:::

# [Demo Day Is Next]{.flow} {.title}

## The format

- **7 minutes** presenting, **3 minutes** of questions, per group
- Order: drawn at random with the `random` module from Session VI
- Show the thing running, your AI disclosure, and one thing that broke
- Everyone in the group has to be there

# [The Work Menu]{.flow} {.title}

## Today

- **Pull before you start, push when you stop.** GitHub is your backup; commit as you go
- Progress today means one working step pushed to GitHub, with commits that tell the story
- I am in the room: use me for blockers, design questions, and "is this scope realistic?"
- Use the agent where it helps, and note down what it did for your disclosure section

## When you're stuck

:::{.callout-tip}
A red traceback you have never seen? Read the last line first, exactly as in Part I. Then, and only then, the agent.
:::

# [Wrap-up]{.flow} {.title}

## Four things to remember

- Rules in `AGENTS.md` for the [always]{.highlight} stuff, skills for the on-demand stuff, both plain markdown you own
- AI text carries a [watermark]{.highlight} now: fluent, normal-looking, detectable by the provider
- The fresh-clone test is the cheapest bug you will ever catch
- A demo is the thing running, the disclosure, and one thing that broke

. . .

Next session: **Demo Day**. The investor is in the audience.
